clue.text: A Scot drunk puts on fat materially

definitions.note: an adverb standing for a noun: 'materially' means 'as a material', i.e. the clue asks for a fabric

indicators.note: one piece is set on, that is after, another, placing the word for fat at the end

parts.note: fou is the Scots word for drunk, so this is how a Scot says it
lard is pig fat

explanation.surface: A tipsy Scotsman piles on the pounds in the most physical sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose by modern standards: the adverb 'materially' points to a material, the silk fabric. 'puts on' places the fat after the Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Foulard is a light silk or silk-and-cotton fabric, a dress and tie material.

clue.text: Old wine makes Alf squiffy, goes to Ernest's head: they finish with a Scotch

indicators.note: the pieces end with the next one, placing it last in the build
squiffy means tipsy, so the letters of the name stagger into a new order

parts.note: the head or opening of the name Ernest gives its first three letters
Ian is the stock Scottish man's name, a Scotsman in old crossword usage

explanation.surface: Alf gets tipsy, the drink goes to Ernest's head, and the session ends on whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'squiffy' shuffles ALF to FAL; 'they finish with' puts IAN, a Scotsman, at the end. 'Scotch' looks like whisky but stands for a Scot.
explanation.definitionFit: Falernian was a celebrated wine of ancient Rome, from the Falernian territory of Campania.

clue.text: Not like a rail crossing

parts.note: a place where a road crosses a railway on the flat has a familiar name; prefix 'not' to its first word

explanation.surface: Something quite unlike the place where road meets railway.
explanation.walkthrough: The British name for a road crossing a railway at grade is a 'level crossing'; something not like one is the opposite of that first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Uneven ground is the opposite of flat, just as a level crossing is flat.

clue.text: Old sort descended from Flood survivors ?

definitions.text: Old sort descended from Flood survivors ?

parts.words: Old sort descended from Flood survivors ?
parts.note: the original pattern of a kind, read also as the 'type' that came out of Noah's vessel, which held the survivors of the Flood

explanation.surface: A primitive breed whose ancestors came off Noah's boat.
explanation.walkthrough: Heard as 'ark type', the word suggests creatures from Noah's Ark; its real sense is the original model from which later sorts derive.
explanation.definitionFit: An archetype is the original model or first pattern, so an ancient sort from which others descend.

clue.text: Middleman in the street

parts.note: the man in the street is 'Tom; the middle one of those three names

explanation.surface: A trader or broker doing business on the high street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middleman' suggests a broker, but it is the middle name of 'Tom, Dick and Harry', the phrase for ordinary people, the men in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: In the trio of everyday names Tom, Dick and Harry, the second sits in the middle.

clue.text: Disinclined for cornets where people are trying to work

definitions.text: where people are trying to work

parts.note: to be off something is to have lost the taste for it
a cornet is an ice-cream cone, so cornets are ices

explanation.surface: Someone who has gone off ice-cream cones, at their desk trying to get work done.
explanation.walkthrough: A cornet here is the British word for an ice-cream cone, not the brass instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Offices are workplaces where staff are busy at their jobs.

clue.text: Seat of learning's latitudinarianism regarding lower members in the cloth

definitions.text: Seat of learning's latitudinarianism regarding lower members in the cloth

parts.words: Seat of learning's latitudinarianism regarding lower members in the cloth
parts.note: a university city's broad-mindedness about legs, read as its famous wide-legged trousers made of cloth

explanation.surface: A university's broad-church tolerance towards junior clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'latitudinarianism' and 'the cloth' sound ecclesiastical, but here latitude is width, lower members are legs, and the cloth is the trousers' fabric. Oxford is the seat of learning.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford bags are very wide-legged trousers fashionable at Oxford University in the 1920s.

clue.text: Lots were appointed by this committee of three

definitions.text: Lots were appointed by this committee of three

parts.words: Lots were appointed by this committee of three
parts.note: in Greek myth three goddesses allot each person's destiny, or lot

explanation.surface: A three-person committee assigning lots at an auction or ballot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lots' looks like auction items, but a lot is one's destiny, assigned by the three goddesses of Greek myth who spin, measure and cut the thread of life.
explanation.definitionFit: Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos were the three goddesses who decided every mortal's destiny.

clue.text: Motor assembly plant ?

definitions.meaning: a factory production line building automobiles
the ... thistle, a spiny plant of the daisy family

explanation.surface: A factory where cars are put together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a factory, part of the motor-assembly picture, but it is the botanical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A production line for automobiles is a car line; the carline thistle is a European wild flower.

clue.text: Equity investment for a turnover in real estate

definitions.meaning: a stake in a company's capital

definitions.text: for a turnover in real estate
definitions.meaning: the blade of a plough, which turns over the land

explanation.surface: A stake bought in a company to profit from property dealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turnover' and 'real estate' sound like business, but the second sense is the ploughshare, which turns over the soil of the land.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock-market holding is a share; a ploughshare is the blade that turns the earth.

clue.text: Time long after Schubert's time

parts.note: a 1920s English operetta built on Schubert's melodies, named for the season of a spring-flowering shrub

explanation.surface: A period long after the composer Schubert lived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lilac Time' is the English title of an operetta written long after Schubert's death using his music; the word before 'Time' is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The shrub whose blossom gives its name to the operetta Lilac Time, staged in London in 1922.

clue.text: Where self-help brings a refreshing result

definitions.text: Where self-help brings a refreshing result

parts.words: Where self-help brings a refreshing result
parts.note: a restaurant where diners serve themselves food and drink

explanation.surface: Self-improvement leading to a reinvigorating outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'self-help' sounds like personal improvement; here it means serving yourself, and 'refreshing' means food and drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-service restaurant where customers help themselves to refreshments.

clue.text: Troupe rather than troop inspections

parts.note: military inspections of troops sound the same as variety shows put on by a troupe of performers

explanation.surface: Inspecting a theatre company instead of a body of soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspections of troops are reviews; theatrical shows by a troupe have a French spelling of the same sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Revues are light stage entertainments of sketches and songs, performed by a troupe.

clue.text: Old pint, sire

annotationWithheld.why: 'Old pint, sire' (8): PRISTINE is an anagram of PINT SIRE with 'Old' as definition, but no clue word signals the anagram (an unindicated anagram, a licence of 1960s puzzles), so the op has no indicator

clue.text: Could be a traumatic event for the Trust

definitions.text: Could be a traumatic event for the Trust

parts.words: Could be a traumatic event for the Trust
parts.note: the Brains Trust was a BBC panel programme; a storm hitting it would be a mental upheaval

explanation.surface: A disaster that might befall a charitable trust.
explanation.walkthrough: The Brains Trust was a popular BBC radio and TV panel answering listeners' questions; a storm for the 'brains' is a sudden mental upset.
explanation.definitionFit: A brainstorm in older usage is a sudden violent mental disturbance.

clue.text: Insular admission of homicide

parts.note: a confession of killing, 'I kill', with a synonym, read as the name of an island

explanation.surface: An islander confessing to murder.
explanation.walkthrough: A confession 'I slay' runs together into the name of a Hebridean island; 'Insular' points to the island.
explanation.definitionFit: Islay is an island of the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland.

clue.text: Bone to pick with a warder of the Tower ?

definitions.text: Bone to pick with a warder of the Tower ?

parts.words: Bone to pick with a warder of the Tower ?
parts.note: a joint to gnaw, and a grievance with one of the yeoman warders, who are called Beefeaters

explanation.surface: Having a grievance against a guard at the Tower of London.
explanation.walkthrough: A bone to pick is a grievance, but here a literal bone; the Tower of London's warders are nicknamed Beefeaters, who would eat this cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A rib of beef is a roasting joint on the bone, food for a beefeater.

clue.text: Mink pants ?

parts.note: trousers of mink would put fur low down; the word also means flounces on a dress

explanation.surface: Trousers made of mink.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'fur below', fur on the legs; the real word means frills and flounces on women's clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Furbelows are ruffles or flounces on a garment, showy trimmings.

clue.text: For Masons' lodges ?

parts.note: a building stone, read as the stone for Freemasons' meeting places

explanation.surface: Something intended for the meeting halls of Freemasons.
explanation.walkthrough: Masons' lodges suggest Freemasons; the stone that cuts freely in any direction, used by stonemasons, carries their 'free' prefix.
explanation.definitionFit: Freestone is fine-grained stone such as sandstone that can be cut easily in any direction.

clue.text: Ned riding to the base

annotationWithheld.why: 'Ned riding to the base' (9): NIDDERING is an anagram of NED RIDING with 'base' as definition, but no clue word signals the anagram ('to the' is a link), so the op has no indicator

clue.text: Darn ! Better contact Battersea

parts.note: Battersea Dogs Home in London takes in lost dogs, so a dog has gone missing

explanation.surface: Damn, someone had better ring Battersea.
explanation.walkthrough: Battersea Dogs Home is London's famous refuge for lost dogs; an owner whose dog has gone calls it, and 'dog gone' is the mild oath.
explanation.definitionFit: Doggone is an American euphemistic exclamation like 'damn', a mild oath.

clue.text: In Polperro guess Ill see a lonesome elephant

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Guessing that in a Cornish fishing village you will see a solitary elephant.
explanation.walkthrough: Polperro is a Cornish fishing village. 'In' signals the run hidden in POLPERRO GUESS.
explanation.definitionFit: A rogue elephant is one that lives apart from the herd and is often savage.

clue.text: Dance up to five in five-bar form

indicators.note: the reversed letters go inside the gate

parts.note: a five-bar gate is a common British field gate

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' sends the letters of 'to five' upwards, backwards

parts.note: taken as written
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: A dance counted up to five in a pattern of five bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns 'to five' backwards, and 'in' puts the result inside the five-bar gate, the common British field gate.
explanation.definitionFit: The gavotte is an old French dance in moderate four-four time.

clue.text: Severe quaker ?

parts.note: a fit of shivering is a rigor, so one who quakes with it; the real sense is a stern stickler

explanation.surface: A stern member of the Society of Friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quaker' suggests the Society of Friends; read as one who quakes, it hints at a rigor, a fit of shivering.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigorist insists on strict observance of rules, so is severe.

clue.text: Receive the nicked razor reconditioned ?

definitions.meaning: in Scots law, to receive stolen goods
a blade put back in sharp order

explanation.surface: Accepting a razor that has been cut and is being refurbished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nicked' looks like a cut razor, but in British slang nicked means stolen; the Scots law term for receiving stolen goods is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Reset is the Scots-law crime of handling stolen goods, and resetting a razor makes it ready again.

clue.text: What a bore the poet can be

definitions.meaning: a tool for enlarging holes, a reamer

explanation.surface: How tedious a poet can be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bore' looks like a tedious person, but it is a boring tool; the poet is a writer of rhymes, in the old spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A rimer is a tool for enlarging holes, and also a variant spelling of rhymer, a versifier.

clue.text: What lots of meat to be the first fruitarian's

parts.note: the verb given without its 'to'
Eve ate the forbidden fruit, the first person to eat fruit, so this is Eve's

explanation.surface: A heap of meat claimed by the first vegetarian.
explanation.walkthrough: Eve, who ate the apple in Eden, is the first fruitarian.
explanation.definitionFit: Beeves is the old plural of beef, meaning oxen raised for meat.

clue.text: Most of the spilt milk's creamless

indicators.note: spilt milk is scattered, so the letters fall into a new order
take most of the word, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: taken with its s

explanation.surface: Most of the milk spilled has lost its cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of the' drops L from MILKS, leaving MIKS, and 'spilt' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: Skim milk has had its cream taken off, so it is without cream.

clue.text: Any port for this old bird ?

definitions.text: Any port for this old bird ?

parts.words: Any port for this old bird ?
parts.note: the proverb 'any port in a storm', with the bird that sings in rough weather

explanation.surface: Any harbour will do for this elderly sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Any port in a storm' means any refuge will do; the mistle thrush, which sings in stormy weather, has a country name built from the storm.
explanation.definitionFit: The stormcock is an old country name for the mistle thrush, which sings in bad weather.

clue.text: Better alfresco entertainment

parts.note: in the open air, out of doors
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Open-air entertainment is preferable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like an adjective but is the verb, to surpass.
explanation.definitionFit: To outdo is to surpass or beat.

clue.text: It's all the more trouble to prove

definitions.note: a phrase standing for a noun: something to be proved

indicators.note: to trouble something is to stir it up, so the letters are disturbed

explanation.surface: Proving it is all the more trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' rearranges THE MORE.
explanation.definitionFit: A theorem is a proposition to be demonstrated by logical proof.

clue.text: Foreign plane, identity unsolved

definitions.meaning: a French jet fighter of the 1950s built by Dassault
the French word for an enigma, an unknown

explanation.surface: An aircraft from abroad whose identity nobody can work out.
explanation.walkthrough: Both definitions are French: the Dassault Mystère jet, and the French word for a mystery.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mystère was a French fighter jet of the 1950s, and mystère is French for an enigma.
